sequences.title: Adding the input $Bu$
sequences.summary: The input term joins the dynamics, and its shapes are forced: $B$ must be $n \times q$ so that $Bu$ is an $n$-vector like $Ax$.

initial.title: Where we were
initial.explanation: The previous lectures studied $\dot x = Ax$: the eigenvalues of $A$ alone decide whether the state decays or grows.

steps.title: Add a control term
steps.explanation: A forcing term $Bu$ is added. $u$ is the signal we choose; $B$ says how it enters each state equation.

steps.title: Shapes of every factor
steps.explanation: $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $u \in \mathbb{R}^q$ ($q$ actuators). For $Bu$ to be an $n \times 1$ column like $Ax$, $B$ must be $n$ tall and $q$ wide: one column per actuator.

steps.title: Assume the full state is measured
steps.tex: y = Cx,\quad C = I \;\Rightarrow\; y = x
steps.explanation: Measurements $y = Cx$ come later. In this lecture $C = I$: every state is available for feedback. (This $C$ is not the controllability matrix $\mathcal{C}$.)

sequences.title: Substituting $u = -Kx$
sequences.summary: Proportional state feedback turns $\dot x = Ax + Bu$ into $\dot x = (A - BK)x$; controllability is about how freely $K$ can move its eigenvalues.

initial.title: System and feedback law
initial.explanation: With the whole state measured, the lecture uses the linear law $u = -Kx$, where $K$ is a $q \times n$ gain matrix.

steps.title: Put $-Kx$ in place of $u$
steps.explanation: The input $u$ is replaced by the feedback $-Kx$. $B$ still acts on it from the left.

steps.title: Pull out the minus sign
steps.explanation: $B(-Kx) = -BKx$. $BK$ is $(n\times q)(q\times n) = n \times n$, the same shape as $A$.

steps.title: Factor $x$ on the right
steps.explanation: Both terms end in $x$, so $x$ factors out on the right. The closed loop is again $\dot x = (\text{matrix})x$ with the new matrix $A - BK$.

steps.title: What controllability promises
steps.explanation: If $(A, B)$ is controllable, a suitable $K$ places the eigenvalues of $A - BK$ anywhere (as conjugate pairs for real matrices), and some input steers $x$ to any point in finite time. Only $A$ and $B$ decide this.

sequences.title: Blocked, more actuators, coupled
sequences.summary: Writing the examples row by row shows when the input can reach every state: never for $x_1$ in the uncoupled case, directly with two actuators, and indirectly through coupling.

initial.title: Uncoupled dynamics, one input
initial.explanation: The lecture's first example: diagonal $A$ with eigenvalues $1$ and $2$ (both unstable) and a single actuator $B = [0, 1]^T$.

steps.title: Expand row by row
steps.explanation: Row 1: $1\cdot x_1 + 0\cdot x_2 + 0\cdot u = x_1$. Row 2: $0\cdot x_1 + 2x_2 + 1\cdot u$.

steps.title: $x_1$ is out of reach
steps.explanation: The $x_1$ equation contains neither $u$ nor $x_2$, so no input affects $x_1$: it grows like $e^t$ regardless. The pair is uncontrollable.

steps.title: Fix 1: a second actuator
steps.tex: B = I:\quad \dot x_1 = x_1 + u_1,\quad \dot x_2 = 2x_2 + u_2
steps.explanation: With $B = I$ each state has its own input, so both can be stabilised independently: controllable. Every column of $B$ is another actuator.

steps.title: Fix 2: coupling, one actuator
steps.tex: A = \begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&2\end{bmatrix}:\quad \dot x_1 = x_1 + x_2,\quad \dot x_2 = 2x_2 + u
steps.explanation: Back to one input $B = [0, 1]^T$, but now $x_2$ drives $x_1$. The input reaches $x_1$ through $x_2$, and the pair is controllable (proved by the rank test later).

sequences.title: The controllability matrix and its rank
sequences.summary: Repeatedly multiplying $B$ by $A$ produces the blocks of $\mathcal{C}$; controllability is the statement that these columns span $\mathbb{R}^n$.

initial.title: Start from the input direction
initial.explanation: Everything is built from $B$, the directions the actuators push, and $A$, which moves those directions around.

steps.title: Multiply by $A$, again and again
steps.explanation: Each block is $A$ times the previous one, with $A$ on the left. The list stops at $A^{n-1}B$: $n$ blocks.

steps.title: Size of $\mathcal{C}$
steps.explanation: Every block has the shape of $B$, $n \times q$. Side by side, $n$ blocks make $n \times nq$; square only for a single input.

steps.title: The rank test
steps.explanation: Controllable exactly when $\mathcal{C}$ has $n$ independent columns, so its columns span $\mathbb{R}^n$: full ROW rank. (The lecture says “full column rank”; that matches only for one input.)

steps.title: Why: kick and let it ring (discrete time)
steps.tex: x_1 = Bu_0,\quad x_2 = ABu_0 + Bu_1,\quad x_3 = A^2Bu_0 + ABu_1 + Bu_2
steps.explanation: Authored illustration with $x_{k+1} = Ax_k + Bu_k$, $x_0 = 0$: each step passes earlier kicks through $A$ once more. Reachable states are combinations of the columns of $\mathcal{C}$.

sequences.title: Computing $\mathcal{C}$: rank 1 versus rank 2
sequences.summary: Multiplying $A$ into $B$ entry by entry for both examples: the uncoupled columns stay on the $x_2$ axis (rank 1), the coupled ones span the plane (rank 2).

initial.title: Uncoupled pair
initial.explanation: The lecture's first example, now tested with $\mathcal{C} = [B\ \ AB]$ since $n = 2$.

steps.title: Multiply $A$ into $B$
steps.explanation: Row times column: top $1\cdot0 + 0\cdot1 = 0$, bottom $0\cdot0 + 2\cdot1 = 2$. So $AB = [0, 2]^T$.

steps.title: Assemble and look at the columns
steps.explanation: $B$ and $AB$ both lie on the $x_2$ axis; $AB = 2B$.

steps.title: Determinant 0, rank 1
steps.explanation: Rank 1 < 2: uncontrollable. More powers do not help: $A^2B = [0, 4]^T$, $[0, 8]^T$, ... keep a zero on top.

steps.title: Coupled $A$, same $B$
steps.explanation: The coupling entry contributes $1 \cdot 1$ to the top row, so $AB = [1, 2]^T$ now has an $x_1$ component.

steps.title: Determinant $-1$, rank 2
steps.explanation: Two independent columns span the plane: rank 2, controllable.

sequences.title: ctrb in MATLAB and the limits of a yes/no test
sequences.summary: The computer reproduces the board, but the rank test is binary and linear: degree of controllability and nonlinear effects need more.

initial.title: The command
initial.explanation: ctrb builds $\mathcal{C}$; rank tests it. Useful when the system is too big to check by hand.

steps.title: The two examples on the computer
steps.explanation: With B = [0; 1], the uncoupled A gives rank 1 (not controllable) and the coupled A gives rank 2 (controllable), matching the board.

steps.title: Linearizations only
steps.explanation: Neglected nonlinear terms may still give control authority, or not; nonlinear controllability is hard in general.

steps.title: Yes/no hides the degree
steps.explanation: Authored comparison: both have rank 2, but a weak coupling leaves one direction barely actuated. The SVD of $\mathcal{C}$ previews this; exact energy measures need the Gramian (later).

steps.title: What comes next
steps.explanation: Following lectures justify the matrix, measure how controllable a system is, and finally design the feedback gain.
